questions.question: What are the seven workbench surfaces that determine whether an agent ships reliably?
options: Model, Prompt, Tools, Memory, State, Output, Logging
Instructions, State, Scope, Feedback, Verification, Review, Handoff
Plan, Execute, Verify, Test, Review, Deploy, Monitor
Input, Processing, Storage, Retrieval, Generation, Evaluation, Output
questions.explanation: The seven workbench surfaces are: Instructions (startup rules, definition of done), State (current task, touched files, next action), Scope (allowed/forbidden files), Feedback (real command output), Verification (tests, lint, smoke run), Review (second pass with different role), and Handoff (what changed, what is left).

questions.question: What evidence-backed claim does Terminal Bench 2.0 provide about harness vs model quality?
options: Models matter 10x more than harness
The same model moved from outside the top 30 to rank 5 on Terminal Bench by changing only the harness
Harness changes have no measurable effect on benchmark scores
Only frontier models benefit from harness optimization
questions.explanation: LangChain's 'Anatomy of an Agent Harness' (April 2026) reports: a coding agent jumped from outside the top 30 to rank 5 on Terminal Bench 2.0 by changing only the harness. Same model. Different surfaces. A 25-rank delta.

questions.question: What failure occurs when the Scope surface is missing?
options: The agent runs out of memory
Edits leak into unrelated code — the agent touches files with no connection to the task
The agent cannot find the relevant files
The agent produces output in the wrong format
questions.explanation: Without the Scope surface (allowed files, forbidden files, acceptance criteria), edits leak into unrelated code. The agent narrates each touch in good faith but collectively produces a different change than what was reviewed.

questions.question: What failure occurs when the State surface is missing?
options: The agent produces incorrect answers
Each session restarts from zero — the next agent rediscovers everything, re-runs the same commands, re-asks the same questions
The agent cannot use external tools
The agent fails to follow the verification step
questions.explanation: Without the State surface (current task, touched files, assumptions, blockers, next action), each session restarts from zero. The agent re-discovers what was already done, re-runs commands, and wastes tokens recovering the previous session's last 30 seconds.

questions.question: What does the Vercel '80% to 100%' receipt illustrate about workbench design?
options: Adding more tools always improves agent performance
Deleting 80% of the agent's tools (reducing scope/surface) moved success rate from 80% to 100% — negative space wins
Larger models solve the tool-selection problem
Performance improvements require fine-tuning on domain data
questions.explanation: Vercel reported deleting 80% of its agent's tools moved success rate from 80% to 100%. A smaller, more focused tool surface with sharper scope means fewer ways to fail. This illustrates that workbench design — specifically scope — has direct impact on reliability.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between workbench and prompt engineering?
options: Workbench is automated; prompt engineering is manual
Prompting tells the model what you want this turn; a workbench tells the agent how to do work across turns and across sessions
Workbench is used for code tasks; prompt engineering is for text tasks
Workbench requires more compute; prompt engineering is cheaper
questions.explanation: Prompting tells the model what you want in this single turn. A workbench tells the agent how to do reliable work across turns and across sessions — state survives, scope is enforced, feedback is captured, verification runs, and handoffs persist. Most agent failure stories are workbench failures wearing prompt-engineering clothes.
